A practical checklist for your next prioritisation meeting Final thoughts Product Management Product Strategy Leadership Startups Ai Product Development The Product Prioritisation Trap: Why Everything Can’t Be a Priority Olivia bennett 5 min read · Oct 15, 2026 -- Listen Share One of the hardest parts of product management isn’t deciding what to build. It’s deciding what not to build. A sales team wants a feature to close a major deal. Customer success wants improvements for existing customers. Engineering wants time to address technical debt. Leadership has a new strategic initiative that suddenly needs attention. Every request has a reasonable argument behind it. The challenge begins when all these requests compete for the same limited resources. When everything becomes a priority, teams lose focus, roadmaps become unpredictable, and even the most capable engineers can spend months delivering work without making meaningful progress towards a clear objective. So how should product managers approach prioritisation when everyone believes their request matters? Press enter or click to view image in full size 1. A loud request isn’t necessarily an important problem In many organisations, the urgency of a request depends on who raises it. A request from a major customer might immediately move to the top of the roadmap. A senior stakeholder’s idea may receive more attention than a recurring problem reported by hundreds of smaller customers. This is understandable. Businesses have commercial commitments, strategic relationships, and deadlines to meet. But prioritising based solely on the volume or seniority of requests creates a reactive product organisation. The better starting point is to understand the problem behind each request. Who experiences it? How frequently does it occur? What happens if it remains unresolved? Does it affect a strategic business objective? A feature request is a proposed solution. It shouldn’t automatically become the problem statement. Sometimes the requested feature is the right answer. Other times, a simpler change can address the underlying issue more effectively. 2. Separate business outcomes from feature delivery A roadmap can look productive while failing to create meaningful business value. Imagine a team planning to launch five new features in a quarter. The team delivers all five on schedule, but customer activation and retention remain unchanged. From a delivery perspective, the quarter was successful. From an outcome perspective, the results are less convincing. This is why product teams should define what they want to improve before committing to a solution. Instead of writing a roadmap item such as “Build an advanced onboarding dashboard”, the team might define an objective around helping new customers reach their first meaningful outcome more quickly. That distinction changes the conversation. The dashboard becomes one possible approach rather than the predetermined answer. The team can explore alternative solutions and measure whether the chosen approach actually improves the experience. Features are important, but they should serve a clear purpose. 3. Use a consistent framework, not a magic formula Product teams often use prioritisation frameworks such as RICE, which considers reach, impact, confidence, and effort. These frameworks can be helpful because they encourage teams to evaluate ideas using consistent criteria. For example: Reach: How many users or customers will this affect? Impact: How significantly could it improve the intended outcome? Confidence: How strong is the evidence supporting the estimate? Effort: What resources will implementation require? However, a prioritisation score should support judgement, not replace it. Estimates are imperfect. A high-impact idea supported by weak evidence may be riskier than a smaller improvement backed by extensive customer research. Some work also has constraints that a simple score may not capture, such as security requirements, contractual commitments, or urgent reliability issues. The purpose of a framework is to make assumptions visible and trade-offs easier to discuss. It isn’t to create a mathematically perfect roadmap. 4. Technical debt deserves a place in the conversation Technical debt can be difficult to prioritise because its cost is often indirect. A customer-facing feature may create immediate, visible value. Refactoring an ageing service might appear to deliver nothing new to users. But delaying technical improvements indefinitely can make future changes slower and riskier. Build times increase. Small changes require disproportionate effort. Incidents become harder to diagnose. Engineering teams spend more time working around existing limitations. Product managers don’t need to make every technical decision themselves, but they should understand the business consequences of these constraints. A useful discussion with engineering might focus on questions such as: Which systems are slowing down planned product work? What risks are increasing over time? How much engineering capacity is being consumed by recurring issues? What future opportunities become easier if this work is completed? Technical debt should compete for attention based on its consequences, not simply because engineering has requested time to address it. 5. Communicating what won’t be built is part of the job Prioritisation becomes much harder when teams treat every decision as a negotiation that must end
